source.title: SPI-Optimizer: An Integral-Separated PI Controller for Stochastic Optimization
source.authors: Dan Wang; Mengqi Ji; Yong Wang; Hao-Qian Wang; Lu Fang

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present; no material truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Compares adaptive optimizers with SGD and momentum SGD using test error, a different study and measurement setup from Wilson et al. 2017.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-error comparisons for Adam and RMSprop in Table 2. Other optimizer comparisons and convergence-speed results are not extracted because they do not bear on the adaptive-optimizer version.
record.test_reason: Table 2 directly compares held-out classification error after training with adaptive optimizers versus SGD and momentum SGD, the same basic method and measure as V4's original comparison. A different benchmark recipe alone does not make this T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors claim SPI reduces momentum-related oscillation without an extra hyperparameter and achieves faster convergence and lower classification error across their tested networks and datasets, reporting up to 40% fewer epochs and 27.5% mean error reduction relative to compared optimizers.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares a proposed optimizer with standard optimizers across image datasets and architectures; it does not reproduce Wilson et al.'s study or its benchmark setup. The paper says results are averaged after 3 runs and, for each optimizer in the WRN experiments, reports the best test accuracy out of 7 learning-rate settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and architecture vary; the adaptive-optimizer pattern differs on MNIST versus CIFAR benchmarks. The paper states that WRN results use the best test accuracy out of 7 learning-rate settings.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Information Photonics, as stated in the supplied metadata
record.problems: The paper gives no error bars or significance tests for Table 2. Hyperparameter tuning details for the adaptive-optimizer comparisons are not fully stated; WRN results select the best test accuracy out of 7 learning-rate settings.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 comparisons for SGD, MOM, NAG, PID and Addsign are not separate rows because the extracted version concerns adaptive optimizers; SGD and MOM values are recorded as the reference in each row. Other optimizer comparisons and convergence-speed figures are outside V4.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.

Language benchmarks; equal or better adaptive-method training performance; controlled limited versus broader tuning; decoupled weight decay; switching to SGD; word-level language-model advantages. The precise tuning budget for Table 2's adaptive methods is not established.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptations that recover large-batch performance.
Controlled dropout comparisons; using dropout in the MNIST CNN does not test its effect.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All Table 2 values match the record. Results are averaged over three runs, but no dispersion or significance tests are reported. The paper is not an original source for V4. Its discussion of adaptive methods having better training performance cites prior work rather than establishing that comparison in its own experiments.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization were not tested.
Network width beyond interpolation was not tested.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity were not tested.
Language benchmarks, training performance, broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, and word-level language models were not tested.
Batch size and large-batch generalization were not tested.
Sharpness and other generalization measures were not tested.
Removing memorized examples was not tested.
